implementation_notes: Ruby has Fibers, the stackful asymmetric coroutine: Fiber.new runs a block with its own stack, Fiber.yield suspends the whole call chain back to the resumer, and Fiber#resume picks it up where it left off - so an ordinary method deep in a call stack can suspend, with no function colouring. Since Ruby 3.0 Fibers are cheap enough (~a few KB) to be used for structured concurrency. Enumerator is the other form: a generator-style lazy sequence built on Fiber, where #next resumes and #peek inspects the next value without advancing. Ruby's Fibers are asymmetric (they yield only to their resumer), so the symmetric transfer C++20 added is not available. Note that a Fiber's stack does not follow it across threads unless it is created with the storage: true flag, and that a blocking call inside a Fiber blocks the thread just as anywhere else.
idiom_name: Fiber (stackful asymmetric coroutine) for structured concurrency; Enumerator (lazy sequence) for pull-based production
code_sketch:
require 'fiber'

# A Fiber is a stackful coroutine: it suspends the WHOLE call stack, so an
# ordinary method deep in a call chain can yield (no function colouring).
fiber = Fiber.new do
  a = Fiber.yield 1          # suspends the entire stack, back to the resumer
  b = Fiber.yield a + 1      # resumed here
  a + b
end
fiber.resume     # => 1
fiber.resume(10) # => 11

# Enumerator is the pull-based sequence built on a Fiber:
enum = Enumerator.new { |y| tree.each { |n| y << n } }   # lazy; consumer pulls
enum.next
enum.peek      # inspect the next without advancing

# A Fiber created without storage: true cannot migrate across threads; a
# blocking call inside a Fiber blocks the thread just as anywhere else.
pitfalls: A Fiber suspends the whole call stack but does not block the thread - the resumer runs. This is not the same as a thread, and code relying on parallelism inside a Fiber will not get it.
A Fiber is asymmetric: it yields only to its resumer, and cannot resume another Fiber directly (the symmetric transfer C++20 added).
A Fiber created without storage: true cannot be resumed from a different thread; passing it across threads raises or corrupts state.
A blocking call inside a Fiber blocks the thread - the event-loop version of the pattern's 'never block the carrier' rule applies.
An Enumerator that is never exhausted keeps its Fiber alive; a Fiber left mid-suspension holds everything it captured.
